idiom_name: hand-written uniform grid of cell structs (fixed arrays or intrusive lists)
implementation_notes: The classic structure is spelled out by hand: a flat or two-dimensional array of Cell structs, each holding a fixed-size array or an intrusive linked list of entity pointers, plus grid_insert/grid_remove/grid_query helpers and an index function that maps a position to cell coordinates. The C standard library offers no spatial container at all, so arrays are the only primitive and all position-to-cell and membership bookkeeping is application code. A hand-rolled uniform grid stays the right default for moving objects with radius-shaped queries; a quadtree or R-tree must be allocated, rebalanced and freed manually and only pays off for large, mostly static geometry sets.
pitfalls: Cell arrays are sized up front: a cell that overflows silently drops members unless it is reallocated or chained, and the grid dimensions must cover the whole world.
Removing an object means finding and unlinking its node; a stale pointer left in a cell crashes the next query, so store ids or give cells a back-pointer to the member.
Nothing prevents two threads from mutating a cell at once; a shared grid needs an explicit lock or per-thread partitions.
